sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Glute Kick Back Machine is an isolation exercise that targets the gluteus maximus through a hip extension movement against a foot platform.

The machine provides a stable, fixed path of resistance, allowing the lifter to focus entirely on contracting the glutes without balance challenges.

It is a popular choice for direct glute work, with adjustable load to scale difficulty across all training levels.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Direct isolation of the gluteus maximus
- Stable platform allows full focus on glute contraction
- Easy to load progressively as strength improves
- Reduced lower back demand compared to free weight hip extension
- Trains each leg independently to fix imbalances
- Beginner friendly with minimal technique requirements
- Excellent for targeted glute hypertrophy work

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Gluteus Maximus

Secondary: Hamstrings, Erector Spinae, Core, Gluteus Medius

sections.heading: Set Up
sections.content:
1. Adjust the machine to fit your height.
2. Ensure the platform or pad is positioned where you can comfortably place your foot while standing on the other leg.
3. Select an appropriate weight on the stack.

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Stand facing the machine, placing the foot of your working leg against the platform or pad.
2. Lean slightly forward for balance, grasping the machine's handles or support bars.
3. Brace the core and keep the support leg slightly bent.

sections.heading: Kick Back
sections.content:
1. Press back with your foot against the platform, extending your leg straight behind you.
2. Drive the movement with your glute, keeping the working leg relatively straight.
3. Hold the contraction briefly at the top of the kick back.

sections.heading: Return and Repeat
sections.content:
1. Slowly return your leg to the starting position, controlling the movement.
2. Keep tension in your glutes throughout the return.
3. Complete all reps on one side before switching legs.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Using momentum or swinging the leg back
- Arching the lower back excessively
- Letting the working leg bend too much
- Failing to control the eccentric portion
- Going too heavy and losing form
- Holding the breath through the rep
- Tilting the hips to lift more weight

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Glute kick back machine
- Athletic shoes for grip
- Optional: Towel for the foot pad
- Optional: Mirror to monitor form

sections.heading: Machine Adjustments
sections.content:
1. Adjust the foot platform to align with your hip when standing tall.
2. Set the chest or hand pad to support your torso comfortably.
3. Select a weight that allows controlled reps through full range of motion.
4. Confirm the locking pin is fully engaged before starting.

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Stance: Support leg slightly bent, foot flat on the floor.
2. Torso: Slight forward lean, ribs stacked over hips, core braced.
3. Working Leg: Foot flat on the platform, leg relatively straight.
4. Hands: Grip the support handles firmly.
5. Head: Neutral, eyes forward.

sections.heading: Similar Exercises
sections.content:
- Cable Glute Kick Back: Cable version of this movement
- Barbell Hip Thrust: Heavy compound glute lift
- Glute Bridge: Bodyweight or loaded hip extension
- Single Leg Glute Bridge: Unilateral floor variation
- Donkey Kicks: Bodyweight kneeling glute kick back
- Romanian Deadlift: Compound glute and hamstring work

sections.heading: Glute Kick Back Variations
sections.content:
Standard Glute Kick Back Machine: Described here
Cable Glute Kick Back: Performed at a cable column with an ankle strap
Resistance Band Glute Kick Back: Standing version using a band
Donkey Kicks: Bodyweight kneeling kick back
Quadruped Glute Kick Back: On hands and knees with optional ankle weight
Hip Extension Machine: Lying or seated machine variation

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Lower Back Pain: Reduce load and avoid arching the back
Knee Pain: Slightly bend the working leg to reduce knee strain
Hip Mobility Issues: Reduce range of motion to a comfortable level
Balance Issues: Hold the support handles firmly and lean into the chest pad
No Machine Access: Use cables, bands, or bodyweight donkey kicks
Beginners: Start light to learn the movement before progressing
